Fanyu Meng’s previous repost of an article by car-audio specialist Kenneth Ward drew plenty of readers, so when Ward published a new one on New Year’s Day, of equally high quality, he shared it too, in the original English.

Ward teaches sound tuning to aftermarket technicians around what he calls the Three Problems of Car Stereo, all caused by our off-center seats. One side is louder, because the near speaker is closer, which pulls the center image toward it. One side sounds different: the near and far speakers sit at very different angles to the listener, so off-axis response differs, and the image wanders left and right with pitch. This is worst with the classic 6.5-inch woofer low in the door paired with a small tweeter, and is eased by three-way systems or wideband drivers aimed up from the dashboard. And one side arrives first, so center-panned content is comb-filtered.

Factory systems handle this in five ways: plain stereo, stereo with a mono center speaker, stereo optimized for the driver with level, delay and EQ (common in the aftermarket, rare from the factory), stereo with phase manipulation for both front seats, and upmixed multichannel systems with a center speaker, a category that also covers Dolby Atmos. Ward’s conclusion: before choosing any tuning technique, decide whether you are tuning for one seat or two.

Shared by Fanyu Meng from a LinkedIn article by Kenneth Ward (January 2024). Read the original.
